text: Clover "Chloe" Delight Esther Eudaly (1969/1970) is an American politician from Oregon who served as Portland's City Commissioner from 2017 to 2021. Eudaly won her position in November 2016 by promising to focus on the needs of renters, people with disabilities, and individuals with lower incomes, running as a tenants' rights advocate and pledging to encourage the construction of lower-cost housing. She was elected to Position 4 on the Portland City Commission and took office with the Office of Neighborhood Involvement, which she renamed the Office of Community & Civic Life (OCCL). Eudaly has a strong opposition to neighborhood associations, stating they "tend to be dominated by older, white homeowners and push their interests rather than the needs of a diverse, growing city." On September 18, 2019, Willamette Week reported that Eudaly sent an angry email to her City Council colleagues threatening political consequences if they did not support her stance on neighborhood associations. The Fair Access In Renting (FAIR) ordinance, which Eudaly introduced and successfully passed in June 2019 after working on it for two years, changed rental application screening in Portland. FAIR requires a first-come-first-serve approach, prioritizes accessible units for people with disabilities, limits landlords from requiring tenant incomes to be 2 to 2.5 times higher than rent, and restricts the use of credit and criminal histories in rental denials. FAIR passed on a 3–1 vote, with Mayor Ted Wheeler and Commissioner Nick Fish voting in favor along with Eudaly, while Commissioner Amanda Fritz voted against it and Commissioner Jo Ann Hardesty was absent. Eudaly voted to defund the Portland police department, but the proposal was defeated 2–3. The ordinance initially passed as a temporary measure set to expire with Portland’s housing emergency declaration in October 2017, but became permanent by unanimous vote in 2018. Rental fees are based on unit size: $2,900 for a studio or single room occupancy, $3,300 for a one-bedroom, $4,200 for a two-bedroom, and $4,500 for a three-bedroom or larger. In 2018, Eudaly became head of the Portland Bureau of Transportation (PBOT), where she spearheaded the Rose Lane Project, announced in June 2019 in response to the Enhanced Transit Corridors Plan adopted by City Council on June 20, 2018. The project includes dedicated bus-only lanes and adjusted traffic signals to give buses head starts at intersections. Trial runs on Southwest Madison Street, Northwest Everett Street, and the Burnside Bridge showed up to 76% reductions in bus delays, with buses crossing the Burnside Bridge nearly two minutes faster. On February 13, 2020, the Rose Lane Project was unanimously approved by Portland City Council. Eudaly grew up near Forest Grove, Oregon, moved to the Portland suburbs at age nine, attended Tigard High School, dropped out, and moved to Portland in 1988. She opened her bookstore, Reading Frenzy, in 1994 and is a founder of the Independent Publishing Resource Center, a maker's space for independent publishers. She resides in the Woodlawn neighborhood, has a son named Henry, and self-identifies as queer. Eudaly lost her November 2020 re-election bid to Mingus Mapps.
